sections.title: Section A — Units I to IV (compulsory)
Section B1 — Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
Section B2 — Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Revaluation — reduction in an existing provision
questions.question: On reconstitution: the building of ₹2,00,000 is appreciated by 10%; the provision for doubtful debts of ₹6,000 is to be maintained at 5% of debtors of ₹80,000; an unrecorded creditor of ₹2,500 is to be recorded; and stock is to be written down by ₹5,000. The profit on revaluation is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹14,500
Step 1: Building +₹20,000
Step 2: Required provision = 5% × ₹80,000 = ₹4,000; existing ₹6,000 → excess ₹2,000 written back (gain)
Step 3: Unrecorded creditor −₹2,500; stock −₹5,000
Step 4: Profit = 20,000 + 2,000 − 2,500 − 5,000 = ₹14,500
Common mistake: Treating the provision change as a loss gives ₹10,500 (A). Ignoring the stock gives ₹19,500 (C). Ignoring the creditor gives ₹17,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Allotment money including premium — share capital credited
questions.question: On the allotment of 20,000 shares of ₹10 each, ₹5 per share is due, including a premium of ₹2. The amount credited to the Share Capital Account by the allotment entry is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹60,000
Step 1: Allotment due = 20,000 × ₹5 = ₹1,00,000 (Share Allotment A/c Dr.)
Step 2: Of this, the premium (20,000 × ₹2 = ₹40,000) is credited to Securities Premium
Step 3: Share Capital is credited with 20,000 × ₹3 = ₹60,000
Common mistake: Crediting the whole amount to share capital gives ₹1,00,000 (A). ₹40,000 (C) is the premium. ₹80,000 (D) has no basis.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Change in ratio — reserve and revaluation retained in the books
questions.question: Asha, Bela and Chaya share profits in the ratio 3 : 2 : 1 and decide to share equally in future. The balance sheet shows a General Reserve of ₹60,000, and the revaluation shows a profit of ₹30,000. The partners want both to remain in the books unchanged and to pass a single adjusting entry. The entry is:
options: A) Chaya's Capital A/c Dr. ₹15,000; To Asha's Capital A/c ₹15,000
B) Asha's Capital A/c Dr. ₹15,000; To Chaya's Capital A/c ₹15,000
C) Chaya's Capital A/c Dr. ₹15,000; To Asha's and Bela's Capital A/cs ₹7,500 each
D) Chaya's Capital A/c Dr. ₹30,000; To Asha's Capital A/c ₹30,000
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Chaya's Capital A/c Dr. ₹15,000; To Asha's Capital A/c ₹15,000
Step 1: Total to be adjusted = ₹60,000 + ₹30,000 = ₹90,000
Step 2: Asha: 3/6 → 2/6 (sacrifice 1/6); Bela: 2/6 → 2/6 (no change); Chaya: 1/6 → 2/6 (gain 1/6)
Step 3: Amount = ₹90,000 × 1/6 = ₹15,000, paid by Chaya to Asha
Common mistake: Reversing the entry gives (B). Treating Bela as sacrificing gives (C). Using 2/6 gives ₹30,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Redemption of debentures at a premium — amount payable
questions.question: A company issued 2,000, 9% debentures of ₹100 each at par, redeemable after 5 years at a premium of 8%. The amount the company must pay at the time of redemption is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹2,16,000
Step 1: Face value = 2,000 × ₹100 = ₹2,00,000
Step 2: Premium on redemption = 8% × ₹2,00,000 = ₹16,000
Step 3: Amount payable = ₹2,16,000 (the ₹16,000 was recorded at issue as Loss on Issue Dr.; To Premium on Redemption of Debentures)
Common mistake: ₹2,00,000 (A) ignores the premium. ₹16,000 (B) is only the premium. Deducting the premium gives ₹1,84,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Divisible profit — loan interest at an agreed rate, quarterly salary
questions.question: A firm's profit before charging interest on a partner's loan is ₹1,50,000. Partner Bharat has lent ₹80,000 to the firm at an agreed interest rate of 9% p.a. for the whole year. Bharat also gets a salary of ₹2,500 per quarter, and interest on capital for all partners totals ₹8,000. The profit available for distribution in the profit-sharing ratio is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹1,24,800
Step 1: Interest on loan (a charge) = ₹80,000 × 9% = ₹7,200 → net profit = ₹1,42,800
Step 2: Salary = 4 × ₹2,500 = ₹10,000; interest on capital = ₹8,000
Step 3: Divisible profit = ₹1,42,800 − ₹10,000 − ₹8,000 = ₹1,24,800
Common mistake: Ignoring the loan interest gives ₹1,32,000 (B). Using 6% instead of the agreed 9% gives ₹1,27,200 (C). Stopping after the loan interest (ignoring salary and interest on capital) gives ₹1,42,800 (D).

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Profits shared in the ratio of opening capitals
questions.question: The deed of Hema and Isha provides that profits are to be shared in the ratio of their capitals at the beginning of the year. On 1 April 2025, Hema's capital was ₹1,20,000 and Isha's ₹80,000. The profit for 2025-26 is ₹75,000. Hema's share of profit is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹45,000
Step 1: Capital ratio = 1,20,000 : 80,000 = 3 : 2
Step 2: Hema's share = ₹75,000 × 3/5 = ₹45,000
Common mistake: Sharing equally (the rule only when the deed is silent) gives ₹37,500 (A). ₹30,000 (C) is Isha's share. ₹75,000 (D) is the whole profit.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Opening capital worked back from interest on capital
questions.question: Interest on Mira's capital for 2025-26 at 10% p.a. amounts to ₹14,000. This includes interest on ₹20,000 of additional capital that she introduced on 1 October 2025. Her capital on 1 April 2025 was:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹1,30,000
Step 1: Interest on additional capital for 6 months = ₹20,000 × 10% × 6/12 = ₹1,000
Step 2: Interest on opening capital = ₹14,000 − ₹1,000 = ₹13,000
Step 3: Opening capital = ₹13,000 ÷ 10% = ₹1,30,000
Common mistake: Dividing the whole ₹14,000 by 10% gives ₹1,40,000 (A). Deducting the full ₹20,000 from ₹1,40,000 gives ₹1,20,000 (B). Adding it gives ₹1,50,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Admission — sacrificing ratio when old partners will share equally
questions.question: Ashwin and Bhola share profits in the ratio 3 : 2. They admit Charvi for a 1/4th share, and Ashwin and Bhola agree to share the remaining profits equally. The sacrificing ratio of Ashwin and Bhola is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 9 : 1
Step 1: New shares: Ashwin = 3/4 × 1/2 = 3/8; Bhola = 3/8; Charvi = 2/8
Step 2: Ashwin's sacrifice = 3/5 − 3/8 = 24/40 − 15/40 = 9/40
Step 3: Bhola's sacrifice = 2/5 − 3/8 = 16/40 − 15/40 = 1/40
Step 4: Sacrificing ratio = 9 : 1
Common mistake: Assuming the old ratio gives 3 : 2 (A). Assuming equal sacrifice because they will share equally gives 1 : 1 (B). 3 : 1 (D) has no basis.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Death — order of the accounting steps
questions.question:
A partner dies during the year. Arrange the following steps in the correct order:
(A) Pay the amount due to the executor
(B) Transfer the balance of the deceased partner's Capital Account to the Executor's Account
(C) Prepare the Revaluation Account
(D) Credit the deceased partner's Capital Account with his share of revaluation profit, reserves, goodwill and profit to the date of death
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (C), (D), (B), (A)
Why: The revaluation result must be found first (C) so that every share due can be credited to the deceased partner's Capital Account (D). Only the final balance is transferred to the Executor's Account (B), from which payment is made (A).
Why not the others: (A) transfers the balance before the adjustments. (B) credits the revaluation share before it is known. (D) pays first.
Key point: Revalue → adjust capital → transfer to executor → pay.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Debentures — presentation in the balance sheet
questions.question: 9% Debentures repayable after five years are shown in a company's balance sheet under:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Non-current liabilities — Long-term borrowings
Why: Debentures are borrowed money repayable after more than 12 months, so they are long-term borrowings.
Why not the others:
(B) Debenture holders are not owners.
(C) They would move to current maturities only in the year before redemption.
(D) They are a liability, not an asset.
Key point: Debentures → long-term borrowings at face value.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Interest on drawings — dates not given, plus one dated drawing
questions.question: During 2025-26, Leela's drawings were ₹24,000, made at various dates that are not known. In addition, she withdrew ₹6,000 on 1 January 2026. Interest on drawings is charged at 10% p.a. Her total interest on drawings is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹1,350
Step 1: When dates are not given, interest is charged for an average of 6 months: ₹24,000 × 10% × 6/12 = ₹1,200
Step 2: The ₹6,000 drawn on 1 January is outstanding for 3 months: ₹6,000 × 10% × 3/12 = ₹150
Step 3: Total = ₹1,350
Common mistake: Applying 6 months to the whole ₹30,000 gives ₹1,500 (B). Charging a full year gives ₹3,000 (C). Ignoring the dated drawing gives ₹1,200 (D).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Super profit — non-trade investments excluded
questions.question: A firm's total assets of ₹6,00,000 include non-trade investments of ₹50,000, and its outside liabilities are ₹1,00,000. Its average profit of ₹72,000 includes ₹4,000 of income from the non-trade investments. The normal rate of return is 12%. Goodwill is valued at three years' purchase of super profit. Its value is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹42,000
Step 1: Capital employed = 6,00,000 − 50,000 (non-trade investments) − 1,00,000 = ₹4,50,000
Step 2: Normal profit = 12% × ₹4,50,000 = ₹54,000
Step 3: Normal average profit = ₹72,000 − ₹4,000 = ₹68,000
Step 4: Super profit = ₹14,000; Goodwill = ₹14,000 × 3 = ₹42,000
Common mistake: Making neither adjustment gives ₹36,000 (B). Adjusting only the capital employed gives ₹54,000 (C). Adjusting only the profit gives ₹24,000 (D).
Key point: Non-trade investments and their income are excluded from BOTH sides.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Retirement — existing goodwill written off and new valuation
questions.question: Kunal, Lata and Manoj share profits in the ratio 2 : 1 : 1. Manoj retires. Goodwill of ₹20,000 appears in the books and is written off, and the firm's goodwill is now valued at ₹60,000 (to be adjusted through capital accounts). The net amount credited to Manoj's Capital Account on account of goodwill is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹10,000
Step 1: Existing goodwill written off in the old ratio → Manoj debited 1/4 × ₹20,000 = ₹5,000
Step 2: His share of the valued goodwill, credited by the gaining partners = 1/4 × ₹60,000 = ₹15,000
Step 3: Net = ₹15,000 − ₹5,000 = ₹10,000 (credit)
Common mistake: Ignoring the write-off gives ₹15,000 (A). ₹5,000 (B) is only the write-off. Using the difference in values (₹40,000) × 1/2 gives ₹20,000 (C).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Nominal value of a share
questions.question: The value printed on a share certificate, on which share capital is calculated, is the share's:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Nominal (face) value
Why: Share capital is always recorded at face value; any amount above it is Securities Premium.
Why not the others:
(A) Market value is the stock-exchange price.
(B) The issue price may include a premium.
(C) Book value depends on net assets.
Key point: Share Capital = number of shares × face value.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Share forfeiture balance — presentation
questions.question: The balance in the Share Forfeiture Account relating to forfeited shares that have NOT yet been re-issued is shown in the balance sheet:
options: A) Under Reserves and Surplus as Capital Reserve
C) Added to the paid-up capital, under Share Capital in the notes
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Added to the paid-up capital, under Share Capital in the notes
Why: Until the shares are re-issued, the amount forfeited is still linked to share capital, so it is added to subscribed capital in the notes to accounts.
Why not the others:
(A) It becomes Capital Reserve only after re-issue.
(B) It is not owed to anyone.
(D) It is an addition, not a deduction.
Key point: Before re-issue → add to share capital; after re-issue → surplus to Capital Reserve.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Premium payable with application — transfer to share capital
questions.question: Ruby Ltd. issued 10,000 shares of ₹10 each at ₹12 per share. ₹5 per share, including the whole premium of ₹2, was payable on application. When the application money is transferred on allotment, the amount credited to the Share Capital Account is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹30,000
Step 1: Application money = 10,000 × ₹5 = ₹50,000
Step 2: Premium part = 10,000 × ₹2 = ₹20,000 → Securities Premium
Step 3: Capital part = 10,000 × ₹3 = ₹30,000 → Share Capital
Common mistake: Crediting all ₹50,000 to capital gives (A). ₹20,000 (B) is the premium. ₹40,000 (D) has no basis.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Partnership deed — contents
questions.question:
Which of the following are usually contained in a partnership deed?
(A) The name and address of the firm and of the partners
(B) The profit-sharing ratio
(C) The rates of interest on capital and on drawings
(D) A requirement that the deed be registered with the Registrar of Companies
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: A deed records the identity of the firm and partners (A), how profits are shared (B), and the rules on interest, salaries and drawings (C), along with other terms such as capital and the procedure on admission or retirement.
Why not the others: Statement (D) is false — a firm may be registered with the Registrar of FIRMS under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932; the Registrar of Companies deals with companies. Options (A), (B) and (D) include it.
Key point: Partnership deed = written terms agreed among partners.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Terms of issue and redemption of debentures
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Terms of debentures)
(A) Issued at par, redeemable at par
(B) Issued at a discount, redeemable at par
(C) Issued at a premium, redeemable at par
(D) Issued at par, redeemable at a premium

List-II (Accounting effect at issue)
(I) No gain or loss on issue
(II) Discount on Issue of Debentures A/c debited
(III) Securities Premium A/c credited
(IV) Loss on Issue of Debentures A/c debited and Premium on Redemption of Debentures A/c credited
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(I), (B)-(II), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV)
Why:
(A) Received = repaid = face value → no gain or loss (I).
(B) Less is received than will be repaid → discount (II).
(C) More is received → Securities Premium (III).
(D) More will be repaid → loss on issue, matched by a redemption-premium liability (IV).
Why not the others: (B) swaps par and discount; (C) swaps discount and premium; (D) swaps premium on issue and premium on redemption.
Key point: Compare the money received with the money to be repaid.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Premium for goodwill paid privately
questions.question: A new partner pays his share of goodwill privately to the old partners, outside the business. In the firm's books:
options: A) Cash A/c Dr.; To Premium for Goodwill A/c
C) Goodwill A/c Dr.; To Old Partners' Capital A/cs
D) New Partner's Capital A/c Dr.; To Old Partners' Capital A/cs
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) No entry is passed
Why: The money never enters the firm; it passes directly between the partners as a private arrangement, so the firm records nothing.
Why not the others: (A) applies when the premium is brought INTO the firm. (C) raises goodwill, which is not done. (D) applies when the premium is not brought in and is adjusted through capital accounts.
Key point: Paid privately → no entry in the firm's books.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Issue of shares at a discount — Section 53
questions.question:
Assertion (A): A company cannot issue its shares at a discount, except in the case of sweat equity shares.
Reason (R): Section 53 of the Companies Act, 2013 prohibits the issue of shares at a discount.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
B) Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
C) Assertion is true, but Reason is false
D) Assertion is false, but Reason is true
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
Why: Section 53 declares any issue of shares at a discount void, with the only exception being sweat equity shares issued under Section 54. The legal prohibition (R) is exactly why the company cannot do it (A).
Why not the others: (B) The Reason is the explanation. (C) and (D) Both statements are true.
Key point: Shares — no discount (except sweat equity); debentures — discount allowed.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Goodwill — purchased and self-generated
questions.question: Goodwill that is recorded because a business was bought for a price higher than the value of its net assets is called:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Purchased goodwill
Why: When consideration paid exceeds the net assets acquired, the excess is purchased goodwill, and AS 26 allows only purchased goodwill to be recorded in the books.
Why not the others:
(A) Self-generated goodwill is built internally over time and is not recorded.
(B) Hidden goodwill is inferred from a new partner's capital contribution.
(C) When the price is LOWER than net assets, the difference is a capital reserve, not goodwill.
Key point: Only purchased goodwill appears in the books.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Private placement of securities
questions.question: An offer of securities to a select group of persons, other than by a public offer, through a private placement offer letter under Section 42 of the Companies Act, 2013, is called:
options: C) An Employee Stock Option Plan
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) A private placement
Why: Section 42 permits a company to raise funds from a select group (in a financial year, to not more than 200 persons, excluding qualified institutional buyers and employees under ESOP), using a private placement offer letter.
Why not the others:
(A) A rights issue goes to existing shareholders.
(B) A bonus issue is free and out of reserves.
(C) An ESOP is for employees.
Key point: Select group + offer letter = private placement.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Shares issued for consideration other than cash — accounting
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about shares issued to a vendor for an asset:
(A) The asset is first debited and the vendor credited.
(B) When shares are issued at a premium, the vendor is debited and Share Capital and Securities Premium are credited.
(C) Such shares are disclosed in the notes as shares issued for consideration other than cash.
(D) No journal entry is needed because no cash is received.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: The purchase is recorded first — Asset A/c Dr.; To Vendor (A). The payment by shares then discharges the vendor — Vendor Dr.; To Share Capital and To Securities Premium (B). Schedule III requires disclosure of shares allotted for consideration other than cash (C).
Why not the others: Statement (D) is false — the absence of cash does not remove the need to record the transaction. Options (A), (B) and (D) include it.
Key point: Non-cash issue: two entries, plus a note.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Change in profit-sharing ratio — principles
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about a change in the profit-sharing ratio among existing partners:
(A) The gaining partner compensates the sacrificing partner for goodwill.
(B) Assets and liabilities may be revalued.
(C) Accumulated profits and reserves are distributed in the old ratio.
(D) A new partner is admitted at the same time.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: A change in ratio creates gains and sacrifices, so goodwill is adjusted between them (A); revaluation records value changes up to the date of change (B); and past profits belong to the partners in the old ratio (C).
Why not the others: Statement (D) is false — a change in ratio involves only the existing partners; no new partner is needed. Options (A), (C) and (D) include it.
Key point: Change in ratio = reconstitution without any change in membership.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Guarantee of minimum profit after interest and salary
questions.question: Amar, Bijoy and Chitra share profits in the ratio 2 : 2 : 1. The deed allows interest on capital of ₹20,000, ₹15,000 and ₹10,000 respectively, and a salary of ₹15,000 to Chitra. Chitra is guaranteed a minimum share of profit of ₹30,000 (excluding her interest and salary); any deficiency is borne by Amar and Bijoy in the ratio 3 : 2. The firm's profit is ₹2,00,000. Amar's final share of profit (excluding his interest) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹54,800
Step 1: Divisible profit = 2,00,000 − 45,000 (interest) − 15,000 (salary) = ₹1,40,000
Step 2: Shares 2 : 2 : 1 → Amar ₹56,000; Bijoy ₹56,000; Chitra ₹28,000
Step 3: Chitra's deficiency = ₹30,000 − ₹28,000 = ₹2,000; Amar bears 3/5 = ₹1,200
Step 4: Amar = ₹56,000 − ₹1,200 = ₹54,800
Common mistake: Ignoring the guarantee gives ₹56,000 (A). Sharing the deficiency equally gives ₹55,000 (B). Charging Amar the whole deficiency gives ₹54,000 (C).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Shares versus debentures
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) Debenture holders are creditors of the company, while shareholders are its owners.
(B) Interest on debentures is a charge against profit, while dividend is an appropriation of profit.
(C) Debentures may be secured by a charge on assets; shares are never secured.
(D) Like debentures, shares may freely be issued at a discount.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: Debenture holders lend and shareholders own (A); interest must be paid regardless of profit, while dividend depends on profit (B); and only debentures can carry a charge on assets (C).
Why not the others: Statement (D) is false — Section 53 of the Companies Act, 2013 prohibits issuing shares at a discount (except sweat equity shares), whereas debentures may be issued at a discount. Options (A), (B) and (D) include it.
Key point: Debentures: creditors, interest, security, discount allowed.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Change in ratio — accumulated profits in old ratio
questions.question:
Assertion (A): When partners change their profit-sharing ratio, accumulated profits and reserves are distributed in the old ratio.
Reason (R): These profits were earned while the old ratio was in force.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
B) Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
C) Assertion is true, but Reason is false
D) Assertion is false, but Reason is true
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
Why: Reserves and undistributed profits relate to the period before the change. Since they were earned under the old ratio (R), fairness requires sharing them in that ratio (A); otherwise the gaining partner would benefit from past profits.
Why not the others: (B) The Reason directly explains the Assertion. (C) and (D) Both statements are true.
Key point: Past results → old ratio; future results → new ratio.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Goodwill — average profit after correcting undervalued closing stock
questions.question: A firm's profits for the last three years were ₹50,000, ₹60,000 and ₹70,000. It is found that the closing stock of the LAST year was undervalued by ₹6,000. Goodwill is valued at two years' purchase of the average profit. Its value is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹1,24,000
Step 1: Undervalued closing stock understates that year's profit → corrected profit = ₹70,000 + ₹6,000 = ₹76,000
Step 2: Average profit = (50,000 + 60,000 + 76,000) ÷ 3 = ₹62,000
Step 3: Goodwill = ₹62,000 × 2 = ₹1,24,000
Common mistake: Ignoring the error gives ₹1,20,000 (A). ₹62,000 (B) is the average profit. Adding ₹6,000 to every year gives ₹1,32,000 (C).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Excess application money adjusted towards allotment and call
questions.question: Galaxy Ltd. received applications for 50,000 shares against 20,000 shares offered and allotted pro rata to all applicants. The amounts payable were ₹4 on application, ₹3 on allotment and ₹3 on the first and final call. Its Articles permit excess application money to be adjusted against both allotment and calls. The cash received when the first and final call is made is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Nil
Step 1: Excess application money = (50,000 − 20,000) × ₹4 = ₹1,20,000
Step 2: Allotment due = 20,000 × ₹3 = ₹60,000 → fully adjusted; excess left = ₹60,000
Step 3: Call due = 20,000 × ₹3 = ₹60,000 → fully adjusted from the remaining excess
Step 4: Cash received on the call = Nil (the ₹60,000 held for the call is calls in advance until the call is made)
Common mistake: Ignoring the adjustment gives ₹60,000 (A). ₹20,000 (C) has no basis. ₹1,20,000 (D) is the total excess.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Death — profit to date of death on the average of past profits
questions.question: Ujjwal, a partner with a 1/5th share, died on 30 June 2026. The firm closes its books on 31 March, and his share of profit to the date of death is to be based on the average profit of the last three years: ₹60,000, ₹80,000 and ₹1,00,000. His share of profit is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹4,000
Step 1: Average profit = (60,000 + 80,000 + 1,00,000) ÷ 3 = ₹80,000
Step 2: Profit for 3 months (1 April–30 June) = ₹80,000 × 3/12 = ₹20,000
Step 3: Ujjwal's share = ₹20,000 × 1/5 = ₹4,000
Common mistake: Using the last year's profit (₹1,00,000) gives ₹5,000 (B). His share for a full year gives ₹16,000 (C). ₹20,000 (D) is the whole firm's profit for 3 months.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Interest on drawings — goods withdrawn for personal use
questions.question: On 1 December 2025, partner Kabir took goods costing ₹12,000 from the firm's stock for his personal use. The deed charges interest on drawings at 10% p.a., and the books close on 31 March 2026. The interest charged on these drawings is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹400
Step 1: Goods withdrawn for personal use are drawings, recorded at cost (Kabir's Drawings A/c Dr.; To Purchases A/c ₹12,000)
Step 2: Period from 1 December to 31 March = 4 months
Step 3: Interest = ₹12,000 × 10% × 4/12 = ₹400
Common mistake: Charging a full year gives ₹1,200 (A). Using 6 months gives ₹600 (B). Using 3 months gives ₹300 (C).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Retirement — amount due with accumulated loss, revaluation loss and goodwill
questions.question: Nisha, who has a 1/3rd share, retires. Her capital is ₹50,000 and her drawings for the current period are ₹3,000. The balance sheet shows a DEBIT balance of ₹15,000 in the Profit and Loss Account, and revaluation shows a loss of ₹6,000. The firm's goodwill is valued at ₹45,000. The amount due to Nisha is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹55,000
Step 1: Capital = ₹50,000
Step 2: Less share of P&L debit balance (1/3 × ₹15,000) = −₹5,000
Step 3: Less share of revaluation loss (1/3 × ₹6,000) = −₹2,000
Step 4: Add share of goodwill (1/3 × ₹45,000) = +₹15,000
Step 5: Less drawings = −₹3,000 → ₹55,000
Common mistake: Treating the P&L debit balance as a credit gives ₹65,000 (A). Ignoring drawings gives ₹58,000 (B). Ignoring goodwill gives ₹40,000 (C).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Accumulated profits, losses and reserves on admission
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II on the admission of a partner:

List-I (Item in the balance sheet)
(A) General Reserve
(B) Advertisement Suspense (deferred revenue expenditure)
(C) Investment Fluctuation Reserve, when the fall in value of investments is less than the reserve
(D) Workmen compensation claim exceeding the Workmen Compensation Reserve

List-II (Treatment)
(I) Debited to the old partners' Capital Accounts
(II) Credited in full to the old partners' Capital Accounts
(III) Partly used to meet the fall in value; the balance credited to the old partners
(IV) Excess of the claim debited to the Revaluation Account
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV)
Why:
(A) General Reserve is a past profit → credited to the old partners (II).
(B) Deferred revenue expenditure is a past loss → debited to them (I).
(C) The reserve first absorbs the fall in value; any surplus goes to the old partners (III).
(D) A claim larger than the reserve is an extra liability → the excess is a revaluation loss (IV).
Why not the others: (A) swaps reserve and suspense; (B) swaps suspense and the fluctuation reserve; (D) swaps reserve and the excess claim.
Key point: Past profits → credit old partners; past losses → debit old partners (old ratio).

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Liability of partners
questions.question: The liability of the partners of an ordinary partnership firm for the debts of the firm is:
options: A) Limited to the capital each has contributed
C) Limited to their share of profits
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Unlimited, joint and several
Why: Under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, every partner is liable jointly with all the other partners and also individually (severally) for all acts of the firm done while he is a partner. If the firm's assets fall short, creditors can recover from the partners' private assets.
Why not the others: (A) and (D) describe companies limited by shares or by guarantee. (C) There is no such limit.
Key point: Partnership → unlimited liability; company → limited liability.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Interest on debentures — accrued at the year end
questions.question: Orbit Ltd. issued 10% debentures of ₹6,00,000 on 1 August 2025, with interest payable half-yearly on 31 January and 31 July. Its year ends on 31 March. The interest accrued but not due on 31 March 2026, shown under Other current liabilities, is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹10,000
Step 1: Interest paid on 31 January 2026 for 1 August–31 January = ₹6,00,000 × 10% × 6/12 = ₹30,000
Step 2: Interest for February and March (2 months), not yet due = ₹6,00,000 × 10% × 2/12 = ₹10,000
Step 3: This ₹10,000 is accrued but not due at the year end
Common mistake: ₹40,000 (A) is the total interest expense for 2025-26. ₹30,000 (C) is the amount already paid. ₹60,000 (D) is a full year's interest.

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Partner's loan on dissolution
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

Ravi, Sunil and Tara share profits in the ratio 2 : 2 : 1. They dissolve their firm on 31 March 2026, when the balance sheet shows:
Liabilities — Creditors ₹48,000; Ravi's Loan ₹25,000; Capitals: Ravi ₹90,000, Sunil ₹60,000, Tara ₹35,000.
Assets — Bank ₹8,000; Debtors ₹54,000; Inventory ₹76,000; Furniture ₹40,000; Machinery ₹80,000.
On dissolution: debtors realised ₹51,000; inventory ₹70,000; furniture ₹31,000; and machinery ₹72,000. Shares of another company, which had been written off in the books earlier, were taken over by Tara at ₹9,000. Creditors accepted ₹46,500 in full settlement, and realisation expenses of ₹2,500 were paid by the firm.

Question: How will Ravi's loan of ₹25,000 be dealt with?
options: A) Transferred to the credit side of the Realisation Account
B) Paid in cash after the creditors and before the partners' capitals
C) Transferred to Ravi's Capital Account
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Paid in cash after the creditors and before the partners' capitals
Why: Under Section 48, a partner's loan ranks after outside debts but before capital. It is NOT transferred to the Realisation Account: Ravi's Loan A/c Dr. ₹25,000; To Bank A/c ₹25,000.
Why not the others: (A) Only outside liabilities go to the Realisation A/c. (C) The loan is settled separately from capital. (D) Outsiders come first.
Key point: Partner's loan → paid directly, second in order.

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Asset written off earlier, taken over by a partner
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

Ravi, Sunil and Tara share profits in the ratio 2 : 2 : 1. They dissolve their firm on 31 March 2026, when the balance sheet shows:
Liabilities — Creditors ₹48,000; Ravi's Loan ₹25,000; Capitals: Ravi ₹90,000, Sunil ₹60,000, Tara ₹35,000.
Assets — Bank ₹8,000; Debtors ₹54,000; Inventory ₹76,000; Furniture ₹40,000; Machinery ₹80,000.
On dissolution: debtors realised ₹51,000; inventory ₹70,000; furniture ₹31,000; and machinery ₹72,000. Shares of another company, which had been written off in the books earlier, were taken over by Tara at ₹9,000. Creditors accepted ₹46,500 in full settlement, and realisation expenses of ₹2,500 were paid by the firm.

Question: The journal entry for the shares taken over by Tara is:
options: A) Realisation A/c Dr. ₹9,000; To Tara's Capital A/c ₹9,000
B) No entry, because the shares are not in the books
C) Tara's Capital A/c Dr. ₹9,000; To Realisation A/c ₹9,000
D) Investments A/c Dr. ₹9,000; To Tara's Capital A/c ₹9,000
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Tara's Capital A/c Dr. ₹9,000; To Realisation A/c ₹9,000
Why: The shares had been written off, so they were never debited to the Realisation Account. Tara receives them worth ₹9,000 instead of cash, so the firm gains — Realisation A/c is credited and Tara's Capital debited.
Why not the others: (A) is the entry for a liability taken over by a partner. (B) ignores a real gain. (D) opens an asset account that is not needed on dissolution.
Key point: An unrecorded asset taken by a partner → Partner's Capital Dr.; To Realisation.

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Loss on realisation
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

Ravi, Sunil and Tara share profits in the ratio 2 : 2 : 1. They dissolve their firm on 31 March 2026, when the balance sheet shows:
Liabilities — Creditors ₹48,000; Ravi's Loan ₹25,000; Capitals: Ravi ₹90,000, Sunil ₹60,000, Tara ₹35,000.
Assets — Bank ₹8,000; Debtors ₹54,000; Inventory ₹76,000; Furniture ₹40,000; Machinery ₹80,000.
On dissolution: debtors realised ₹51,000; inventory ₹70,000; furniture ₹31,000; and machinery ₹72,000. Shares of another company, which had been written off in the books earlier, were taken over by Tara at ₹9,000. Creditors accepted ₹46,500 in full settlement, and realisation expenses of ₹2,500 were paid by the firm.

Question: After recording every realisation item, the Realisation Account shows a loss of:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹18,000
Step 1: Debit side = debtors 54,000 + inventory 76,000 + furniture 40,000 + machinery 80,000 + creditors paid 46,500 + expenses 2,500 = ₹2,99,000
Step 2: Credit side = creditors 48,000 + debtors 51,000 + inventory 70,000 + furniture 31,000 + machinery 72,000 + shares taken by Tara 9,000 = ₹2,81,000
Step 3: Loss = ₹2,99,000 − ₹2,81,000 = ₹18,000 (Ravi ₹7,200; Sunil ₹7,200; Tara ₹3,600)
Common mistake: Ignoring the shares taken by Tara gives ₹27,000 (A). Ignoring the expenses gives ₹15,500 (C). Ignoring the discount from creditors gives ₹19,500 (D).

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Final payment to a partner who took over an asset
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

Ravi, Sunil and Tara share profits in the ratio 2 : 2 : 1. They dissolve their firm on 31 March 2026, when the balance sheet shows:
Liabilities — Creditors ₹48,000; Ravi's Loan ₹25,000; Capitals: Ravi ₹90,000, Sunil ₹60,000, Tara ₹35,000.
Assets — Bank ₹8,000; Debtors ₹54,000; Inventory ₹76,000; Furniture ₹40,000; Machinery ₹80,000.
On dissolution: debtors realised ₹51,000; inventory ₹70,000; furniture ₹31,000; and machinery ₹72,000. Shares of another company, which had been written off in the books earlier, were taken over by Tara at ₹9,000. Creditors accepted ₹46,500 in full settlement, and realisation expenses of ₹2,500 were paid by the firm.

Question: The cash finally paid to Tara is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹22,400
Step 1: Capital ₹35,000
Step 2: Less share of realisation loss (1/5 × ₹18,000) = −₹3,600
Step 3: Less shares taken over = −₹9,000
Step 4: Cash paid = ₹22,400
Common mistake: Not deducting the shares gives ₹31,400 (A). Using a 2/5 share of the loss gives ₹18,800 (B). Ignoring the loss gives ₹26,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Total payment to a partner with a loan
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

Ravi, Sunil and Tara share profits in the ratio 2 : 2 : 1. They dissolve their firm on 31 March 2026, when the balance sheet shows:
Liabilities — Creditors ₹48,000; Ravi's Loan ₹25,000; Capitals: Ravi ₹90,000, Sunil ₹60,000, Tara ₹35,000.
Assets — Bank ₹8,000; Debtors ₹54,000; Inventory ₹76,000; Furniture ₹40,000; Machinery ₹80,000.
On dissolution: debtors realised ₹51,000; inventory ₹70,000; furniture ₹31,000; and machinery ₹72,000. Shares of another company, which had been written off in the books earlier, were taken over by Tara at ₹9,000. Creditors accepted ₹46,500 in full settlement, and realisation expenses of ₹2,500 were paid by the firm.

Question: The total cash paid to Ravi on dissolution (for his loan and his capital) is:

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Liquidity ratios — ideal quick ratio
questions.question: The generally accepted ideal (standard) quick ratio is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 1 : 1
Why: Quick assets exclude inventory and prepaid expenses, so a ratio of 1 : 1 means the business can pay its current liabilities from its most liquid assets.
Why not the others: (B) 2 : 1 is the standard current ratio. (C) and (D) are not accepted norms.
Key point: Current ratio 2 : 1; quick ratio 1 : 1.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Trade receivables — working back from the collection period
questions.question: A firm's total revenue from operations is ₹8,00,000, and its credit sales are three times its cash sales. Its average collection period is 1.5 months. Its average trade receivables are:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹75,000
Step 1: Credit sales = 3/4 × ₹8,00,000 = ₹6,00,000
Step 2: Receivables turnover = 12 ÷ 1.5 = 8 times
Step 3: Average receivables = ₹6,00,000 ÷ 8 = ₹75,000
Common mistake: Using total revenue gives ₹1,00,000 (A). Dividing credit sales by 12 gives ₹50,000 (B). ₹1,20,000 (D) has no basis.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Solvency ratios — debentures issued to redeem preference shares
questions.question: A company has equity share capital of ₹4,00,000, preference share capital of ₹1,00,000, reserves of ₹1,00,000 and debentures of ₹2,00,000. It issues further debentures of ₹1,00,000 and uses the money to redeem all its preference shares. Its debt-equity ratio after this is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 0.6 : 1
Step 1: Before: Shareholders' funds = 4,00,000 + 1,00,000 + 1,00,000 = ₹6,00,000; debt = ₹2,00,000 (ratio 0.33 : 1)
Step 2: After: Shareholders' funds = ₹5,00,000 (preference capital redeemed); debt = ₹3,00,000
Step 3: Debt-equity = ₹3,00,000 ÷ ₹5,00,000 = 0.6 : 1
Common mistake: 0.33 : 1 (A) is the ratio before the change. Changing only one side gives 0.5 : 1 (B). Using equity share capital alone gives 0.75 : 1 (C).

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Ratios — numerators
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Ratio)
(A) Operating ratio
(B) Interest coverage ratio
(C) Proprietary ratio
(D) Trade receivables turnover ratio

List-II (Numerator)
(I) Cost of revenue from operations + Operating expenses
(II) Profit before interest and tax
(III) Shareholders' funds
(IV) Credit revenue from operations
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(I), (B)-(II), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV)
Why:
(A) Operating ratio = Operating cost ÷ Revenue (I).
(B) Interest coverage = PBIT ÷ Interest on long-term debt (II).
(C) Proprietary ratio = Shareholders' funds ÷ Total assets (III).
(D) Receivables turnover = Credit revenue ÷ Average trade receivables (IV).
Why not the others: (A) swaps the operating ratio and interest coverage; (C) swaps interest coverage and proprietary; (D) swaps the operating ratio and receivables turnover.
Key point: Know each ratio's numerator AND denominator.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Comparative statement — percentage change
questions.question: In the comparative statement of profit and loss of Zeta Ltd., revenue from operations was ₹4,00,000 in 2024-25 and ₹5,00,000 in 2025-26. The percentage change shown is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 25%
Step 1: Absolute change = ₹5,00,000 − ₹4,00,000 = ₹1,00,000
Step 2: Percentage change = ₹1,00,000 ÷ ₹4,00,000 (the PREVIOUS year) × 100 = 25%
Common mistake: Dividing by the current year gives 20% (A). ₹1,00,000 (C) is the absolute change. 125% (D) is the current year as a percentage of the previous year.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Solvency ratios — debt-equity worked from total assets
questions.question: A company's total assets are ₹10,00,000, its current liabilities ₹2,00,000 and its long-term borrowings ₹3,00,000; the rest is shareholders' funds. Its debt-equity ratio is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 0.6 : 1
Step 1: Shareholders' funds = ₹10,00,000 − ₹2,00,000 − ₹3,00,000 = ₹5,00,000
Step 2: Debt-equity = Long-term debt ÷ Equity = ₹3,00,000 ÷ ₹5,00,000 = 0.6 : 1
Common mistake: Dividing by total assets gives 0.3 : 1 (A). Dividing by capital employed (₹8,00,000) gives 0.375 : 1 (B). Inverting gives 1.67 : 1 (C).

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Common-size statements — features
questions.question:
Which of the following statements about common-size statements are correct?
(A) Each item is shown as a percentage of a common base.
(B) They help compare firms of different sizes.
(C) In a common-size balance sheet, total assets are taken as 100.
(D) They show the absolute change in each item between two years.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: Expressing items as percentages of a base (A), such as total assets = 100 (C), removes the effect of size and allows inter-firm comparison (B).
Why not the others: Statement (D) is false — absolute change between years is shown in COMPARATIVE statements. Options (B), (C) and (D) include it.
Key point: Common-size → proportions; comparative → changes.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Cash flow from operating activities — working capital changes
questions.question: Net profit before tax is ₹1,50,000. During the year, prepaid expenses increased by ₹4,000, outstanding expenses decreased by ₹3,000, trade payables increased by ₹10,000 and inventories decreased by ₹6,000. Cash generated from operations (before tax) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹1,59,000
Step 1: Increase in prepaid expenses (current asset up) → −₹4,000
Step 2: Decrease in outstanding expenses (current liability down) → −₹3,000
Step 3: Increase in trade payables → +₹10,000; decrease in inventories → +₹6,000
Step 4: 1,50,000 − 4,000 − 3,000 + 10,000 + 6,000 = ₹1,59,000
Common mistake: Adding the fall in outstanding expenses gives ₹1,65,000 (B). Deducting the fall in inventories gives ₹1,47,000 (C). Deducting the rise in payables gives ₹1,39,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Operating ratio — working back to cost of revenue
questions.question: A company's revenue from operations is ₹6,00,000 and its operating ratio is 75%. Its operating expenses are ₹80,000. Its cost of revenue from operations is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹3,70,000
Step 1: Operating cost = 75% × ₹6,00,000 = ₹4,50,000
Step 2: Operating cost = Cost of revenue + Operating expenses → Cost of revenue = ₹4,50,000 − ₹80,000 = ₹3,70,000
Common mistake: ₹4,50,000 (A) is the total operating cost. Adding the expenses gives ₹5,30,000 (B). ₹1,50,000 (D) is the operating profit.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Schedule III — cheques in hand
questions.question: As per Schedule III, cheques received from customers but not yet deposited in the bank (cheques in hand) are shown under:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Cash and cash equivalents
Why: Schedule III lists the components of cash and cash equivalents as balances with banks, cheques and drafts on hand, cash on hand, and others. A cheque in hand is as good as cash.
Why not the others:
(A) The customer has already paid by cheque, so the amount is no longer a receivable.
(B) and (D) are for advances and other items.
Key point: Cash on hand + cheques on hand + bank balances = cash and cash equivalents.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Depreciation schedule — written down value after three years
questions.question: A depreciation schedule charges 20% p.a. on the OPENING book value of a machine costing ₹2,50,000 (written down value method), with the formula =opening value × 20% in each row. The book value at the end of the third year is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹1,28,000
Step 1: Year 1: ₹2,50,000 − ₹50,000 = ₹2,00,000
Step 2: Year 2: ₹2,00,000 − ₹40,000 = ₹1,60,000
Step 3: Year 3: ₹1,60,000 − ₹32,000 = ₹1,28,000
Common mistake: Using 20% of cost every year (straight line) gives ₹1,00,000 (A). ₹1,60,000 (B) is the value after two years. ₹32,000 (D) is the third year's depreciation.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Electronic spreadsheet — YEAR function
questions.question: Cell A2 contains the date 15-Aug-2026 (entered as a date). The formula =YEAR(A2) returns:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 2026
Why: YEAR extracts the year from a date value. It is useful for grouping invoices or assets by year.
Why not the others:
(A) 15 is DAY(A2).
(B) 8 is MONTH(A2).
(C) 'Aug' is a display format, not the result of YEAR.
Key point: DAY, MONTH and YEAR pull out the parts of a date.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Loan repayment schedule — quarterly interest
questions.question: A loan of ₹5,00,000 at 9% p.a. is repaid in quarterly instalments, with interest calculated each quarter on the outstanding balance. In the loan schedule, the interest for the FIRST quarter is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹11,250
Step 1: Quarterly rate = 9% ÷ 4 = 2.25%
Step 2: Interest = ₹5,00,000 × 2.25% = ₹11,250
Common mistake: ₹45,000 (A) is a full year's interest. ₹3,750 (C) is one month's interest. ₹22,500 (D) is half a year's interest.
Key point: In a schedule, the rate must match the period — annual ÷ 4 for quarterly payments.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Electronic spreadsheet — AutoFill
questions.question: An accountant types Jan in one cell and drags the small square at the corner of the cell across to fill Feb, Mar, Apr and so on automatically. This feature is called:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) AutoFill (fill handle)
Why: Dragging the fill handle continues a recognised series (months, days, numbers) or copies a formula to adjacent cells, saving typing in monthly schedules.
Why not the others:
(A) AutoSum inserts a SUM formula.
(C) Paste Special pastes selected attributes, such as values only.
(D) Wrap Text fits long text inside a cell.
Key point: Fill handle = quick series and formula copying.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Electronic spreadsheet — ROUND on a computed amount
questions.question: Cell B2 contains 1,234. The formula =ROUND(B2*12%,0) returns:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 148
Step 1: B2 × 12% = 1,234 × 0.12 = 148.08
Step 2: ROUND to 0 decimal places → 148 (the next digit, 0, is less than 5)
Common mistake: 148.08 (A) is the unrounded value. 149 (B) is what ROUNDUP would give. 150 (D) rounds to the nearest ten.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Electronic spreadsheet — formula bar
questions.question: The part of the spreadsheet window that shows the formula contained in the active cell, rather than its result, is the:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Formula bar
Why: The cell shows the RESULT of a formula, while the formula bar shows the formula itself (for example =B2*12%), where it can be checked or edited.
Why not the others:
(A) The status bar shows information such as the sum of selected cells.
(B) The title bar shows the file name.
(C) The name box shows the active cell's address.
Key point: Check the formula bar to see how a figure was calculated.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Accounting Information System — features
questions.question:
Which of the following statements about an Accounting Information System (AIS) are correct?
(A) It collects and stores data about transactions.
(B) It processes data into useful information.
(C) It provides reports to internal and external users.
(D) It can be used only by large companies.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: An AIS captures transaction data (A), converts it into information such as ledgers and statements (B), and supplies reports to management, investors, lenders and tax authorities (C).
Why not the others: Statement (D) is false — businesses of every size use an AIS, from a spreadsheet-based system to a full ERP. Options (A), (C) and (D) include it.
Key point: AIS = data → information → reports, at any scale.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Electronic spreadsheet — copying a formula with relative references
questions.question: Cell C2 contains =A2*B2. The formula is copied down to cell C5. The formula in C5 will be:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) =A5*B5
Why: Relative references shift with the formula. Moving down 3 rows changes A2 to A5 and B2 to B5, so each row multiplies its own quantity by its own rate.
Why not the others:
(B) would need absolute references ($A$2*$B$2).
(C) Copying does not add $ signs.
(D) Both references change, not just one.
Key point: Relative references adjust; absolute references stay fixed.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Electronic spreadsheet — nested IF for bonus slabs
questions.question: A sales-bonus sheet uses =IF(B2>=100000,B2*10%,IF(B2>=50000,B2*5%,0)). For a salesperson whose sales in B2 are ₹75,000, the bonus is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹3,750
Step 1: First test: 75,000 ≥ 1,00,000? FALSE → move to the inner IF
Step 2: Second test: 75,000 ≥ 50,000? TRUE → B2 × 5%
Step 3: Bonus = ₹75,000 × 5% = ₹3,750
Common mistake: Applying the 10% slab gives ₹7,500 (B). Treating both tests as false gives 0 (C). ₹75,000 (D) is the sales figure.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Payroll — components
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Payroll item)
(A) Dearness Allowance (DA)
(B) House Rent Allowance (HRA)
(C) Provident Fund (PF)
(D) Professional tax

List-II (Description)
(I) Allowance linked to the cost of living
(II) Allowance towards the rent of accommodation
(III) Retirement saving deducted from salary
(IV) Tax on employment levied by a State
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(I), (B)-(II), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV)
Why:
(A) DA compensates for inflation (I).
(B) HRA helps meet house rent (II).
(C) PF is a retirement fund contribution deducted from pay (III).
(D) Professional tax is a State levy on employment (IV).
Why not the others: (A) swaps DA and HRA; (B) swaps HRA and PF; (C) swaps DA and professional tax.
Key point: Allowances are added to pay; PF, professional tax and TDS are deducted.
